candidates.title: Swap answer order and only count consistent LLM-judge verdicts
candidates.rule: When using an LLM as a pairwise judge, call it twice with the two answers in both orders and count a win only if the same answer wins both times; otherwise record a tie. Do not assume a single-order verdict is stable, especially for closely matched models and open-ended writing/knowledge prompts.
candidates.passage: Only GPT-4 outputs consistent results in more than 60% of cases.
candidates.location: Section 3.3, Table 2 (Position bias of different LLM judges)
candidates.finding: On 80 MT-bench first-turn questions with two similar GPT-3.5 answers, order-swap consistency was 23.8% (Claude-v1), 46.2% (GPT-3.5) and 65.0% (GPT-4) with the default prompt. The authors adopt the conservative swap-and-require-agreement procedure for their main experiments; with it, GPT-4 pairwise judgments reach ~85% agreement with human experts on non-tie votes. Position bias was weaker when models differed widely (98.8% consistency for GPT-3.5 vs LLaMA-13B) and stronger on writing/STEM/humanities than math/coding.
workloads: Chatbot Arena crowdsourced pairwise votes (3K sampled)
candidates.conditions: Pairwise comparison prompt (Figure 4); stress test deliberately used two near-identical GPT-3.5 answers at temperature 0.7, which maximizes position sensitivity. Doubles judge API cost.
candidates.limitations: Single paper, 2023-era model snapshots that may not reproduce; consistency is not accuracy; the swap procedure increases tie rate and cost; the hardest case (near-identical answers) overstates bias relative to typical pairs.
candidates.validation_test: On your own task, run an LLM judge on N pairs in both orders; report consistency rate and how many verdicts flip, then compare swap-consistent verdicts against a held-out set of human labels versus single-order verdicts.

reason: The paper runs controlled comparisons of judge-prompt interventions (position swapping, reference-guided vs CoT vs default grading, single-prompt full-conversation multi-turn judging, few-shot) against human expert votes on MT-bench and Chatbot Arena, yielding scoped, actionable harness rules. Scores and bias descriptions alone were excluded.
